name: Card Identifier Is Id Not Number
description: cards.subtypes stores a single comma-joined string without spaces around the commas for multi-subtype cards, e.g. 'Human,Wizard' on 898 of them. Prefer equality subtypes = 'Human,Wizard' over dual LIKE '%Human%' AND LIKE '%Wizard%' when the question lists exact subtypes together, since the substring form also matches every card carrying those subtypes alongside others. cards.side is NULL on the ordinary one-faced printings, 55,455 of the 56,822 rows, and carries a letter only where a single physical card bears more than one face. Two columns can each look like the answer to which cards, and which of them answers turns on how the question picks the cards out. Where it picks them out by something printed on or recorded about the printing — its border colour, its rarity, its frame or full-art treatment, its original type line, its legality in a format, a store identifier — the answer is cards.id, and that holds even where the wording calls them the card numbers or the names of cards; where such a question also asks for a second attribute, the id comes first and the attribute after it. Where instead it picks them out by who made them or by a language they appear in, the answer is cards.name, because there the question asks what a card is called rather than which printings carry a property. cards.number is the collector number printed inside a set, a per-set label such as 4 or 226s that repeats across sets, so it serves as a filter when a question points at a printed number and never as the answer.
sql: SELECT id FROM cards WHERE subtypes = 'Human,Wizard' AND side IS NULL

name: Illustrator With Play Format, Set Name With Total Set Size, Card Types Across Three Columns
description: A question put in two clauses is answered by one row set carrying both, in the order it puts them, and never by the second clause alone. A follow-up sentence opening state the, show his, list the or indicate the appends a column rather than replacing the one already asked for, so the thing the first clause identifies stays in the projection instead of becoming only a filter. Where that first clause picks its subject by a superlative — the artist who drew the most or fewest cards, the set holding the largest number — the subject is the grouped column, the superlative is the aggregate ordered in the direction the wording asks and cut with LIMIT 1, and the second clause's column is read for whichever group the superlative picks. A card's types are split across three columns, types, supertypes and subtypes, so all of a card's types means all three read together rather than the one named types. Where the subject is a set rather than a card, the set is sets.name: set_translations.translation is that set's title rendered in another language, so it names the translation and not the set.
sql: SELECT T1.artist, T2.format FROM cards AS T1 INNER JOIN legalities AS T2 ON T2.uuid = T1.uuid GROUP BY T1.artist ORDER BY COUNT(T1.id) DESC LIMIT 1

name: Set Code By Release Date
description: sets.releaseDate is written ISO as 'YYYY-MM-DD', so a date given any other way, such as 06/09/1997, is that same day rewritten as '1997-06-09' before it is compared. A set's code is written in two places, as sets.code over all 551 sets and as set_translations.setCode over the 1,210 translation rows covering 121 of them. Where a set is identified by something about the set itself — its release date, its type, its name — and its code is what is asked for, the code comes from set_translations.setCode joined to sets on set_translations.setCode = sets.code, which is where a code is stated beside the set it belongs to, rather than from a bare read of sets. Where the question asks for other sets columns in the same breath, such as a base set size beside the code, sets.code is projected directly.
sql: SELECT T2.setCode FROM sets AS T1 INNER JOIN set_translations AS T2 ON T2.setCode = T1.code WHERE T1.releaseDate = '1997-06-09'

name: Yes Or No Label For A Set Or Card Attribute
description: Whether a set was released outside the United States only, whether it exists online, whether it has a title in some language, whether a card is on the reserved list or carries a content warning — each of these is a question about one named card or set, answered by a word rather than by the value it is stored as. When a question asks whether something holds for a named card or set, the answer is the word itself, IIF(<condition>, 'YES', 'NO') in capitals, rather than the stored value behind it such as 0, 1, 'Legal' or a set code that a reader would have to interpret. The label stands alone in the projection, with no set name or code beside it and no DISTINCT, so one row comes back for each matching card. Where the question also asks for columns to be listed, the label is one further column after them. Where it asks to find any rows of a kind if there are any, the true branch returns the identifying value and the false branch returns 'NO'. Whether a set exists in another language is a row in set_translations carrying that language and a translation, while foreign_data holds a card's own printing in another language, so a question about a version of the set reads set_translations. The label form belongs to a question about one named card or set; a question asking whether there is any card meeting a condition, such as any card by an artist in a given format and availability, is answered by listing the cards that qualify, because there the cards are the answer.
sql: SELECT IIF(T2.isOnlineOnly = 1, 'YES', 'NO') FROM cards AS T1 INNER JOIN sets AS T2 ON T2.code = T1.setCode WHERE T1.name = 'Serra Angel'

name: Percentage Of Cards Or Sets With A Given Property
description: What percentage or share of cards or sets is in a language, of a mana cost, of a rarity, story spotlight, textless, online only or otherwise flagged. A share here is a percentage and both of its halves are counts of rows. The divisor counts the rows of the group the share is taken over and the dividend the rows within that group carrying the property, counted conditionally with SUM(CASE WHEN <condition> THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), and the quotient is cast to REAL before being multiplied by 100, since counts are integers and integer division of a smaller by a larger truncates to zero. Which of the conditions a question names is the group and which is the property is what decides the two halves. The group is the one the question is about: the cards or sets its phrasing heads with, or the ones a phrase such as among these, in this set, or for all of these introduces, and that condition belongs in the WHERE clause, restricting divisor and dividend alike. The property is what is then predicated of that group, the clause saying which of them are in a language, carry a mana cost, lack a text box or are of a set type, and it is the one condition tested inside the CASE. Putting both conditions in the CASE and dividing by the whole table answers a different question, the share of all rows carrying both, and the two are far apart: all 104 story spotlight printings have a text box, so the share among them is 100, while the share of all 56,822 printings that are both is 0.18. A measured column summed in place of a count answers a different question: totalling convertedManaCost adds up mana costs where counting the rows counts cards. The two halves also have to stand over the same rows, so a divisor counting distinct cards beneath a dividend counting joined rows compares two populations instead of dividing one, a share taken over a join being a share of the joined rows. Where a question is put with its formula written beside it, in the shape DIVIDE(COUNT(<one thing>), COUNT(<another>)), those two counts are the dividend and the divisor as written, which settles which condition restricts the group and which is counted inside it, and where that settlement disagrees with the way the wording reads it is the formula that holds: the single condition its dividend counts is the one tested inside the CASE, and every other condition the question names restricts the group, even where the phrasing would have made that other condition the property. A share of the cards is a share of the cards table, so the divisor counts cards.id even when the property being counted sits in a satellite table such as foreign_data or legalities: join the satellite to cards and count the cards, rather than reading the satellite on its own, which would take the share over translations or format rows instead of over cards. The same holds of sets, whose shares are counted over sets.id.
sql: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.isReserved = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.id) FROM cards AS T1 INNER JOIN sets AS T2 ON T2.code = T1.setCode WHERE T2.name = 'Mirage'
